key_features.classic_presentation: ONSET: SUDDEN onset during activity - twisting, rolling, or landing awkwardly. Usually during sports, walking on uneven surface, or stepping off curb. LOCATION: Lateral ankle (outside) most common (85%), medial ankle (inside) less common, anterior ankle possible. DURATION: Immediate pain that may worsen over first 24-48 hours. CHARACTER: SHARP initial pain, then THROBBING and ACHING. AGGRAVATING: WEIGHT BEARING, walking, ankle movement, especially inversion (rolling inward). RELIEVING: REST, ICE, elevation, NSAIDs help. TIMING: Immediate pain that peaks at 24-48 hours, then gradually improves over days to weeks. SEVERITY: 4-8/10 initially, improves with rest. ASSOCIATED SYMPTOMS: SWELLING within hours (lateral ankle), BRUISING (ecchymosis) develops over 24-48 hours, STIFFNESS, difficulty walking or bearing weight. May have 'popping' or 'snapping' sound at injury. KEY POSITIVES: Lateral ankle tenderness, swelling, bruising, positive anterior drawer test, positive talar tilt test. KEY NEGATIVES: No bony tenderness over malleoli (rules out fracture), no deformity, no crepitus.

red_flags: Inability to bear weight immediately after injury - possible fracture, needs X-ray
Severe deformity or obvious fracture - obvious ankle fracture, call 911
Numbness or tingling in foot - possible nerve injury or compartment syndrome
Cold, pale, or blue foot - possible vascular injury, call 911
Open wound with bone visible - open fracture, call 911
